notes: About 1 in 4 people on Earth is under 15. High birth rates in Africa and South Asia keep this number significant, though it has fallen from 1 in 3 just 50 years ago.
Around 10% of the world is over 65 — a proportion that will double by 2050 as populations in wealthy nations age rapidly.
For the first time in history, more than half of humanity lives in urban areas. By 2050 that will be closer to 700 out of 1,000.
The world has about 4 doctors per 1,000 people globally, but this hides enormous inequality — some wealthy nations have 35 per 1,000 while some low-income nations have fewer than 0.2.
There are roughly 10 nurses and midwives per 1,000 people globally, forming the backbone of healthcare in most of the world.
Roughly 70 million primary school teachers serve the world's 700 million primary-age students — an average class size of about 24, though in many regions classes have 50+ students.
About 28% of the global workforce is in agriculture, mostly smallholder farmers in Asia and Africa. In wealthy nations this figure is under 5%.
Around 700–900 million people live on less than $2.15 per day (2017 PPP). This figure has fallen dramatically — it was over 1,900 per 1,000 in 1990.
About two-thirds of humanity is now online. The remaining third — mostly in rural sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — are the focus of major connectivity efforts.
About one-third of humanity is still offline. These people, mostly in rural sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — are the focus of major connectivity efforts.
More than half of all people now carry a smartphone — a technology that barely existed 20 years ago. Mobile phones have leapfrogged wired infrastructure in the developing world.
Global adult literacy stands at around 87%. The 13% who cannot read are concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and among women in conservative regions.
The world produces enough food — about 2,850 calories per person per day — to feed everyone. Hunger persists due to distribution failures, poverty, and waste, not global scarcity.
About 1.3 billion tonnes of food — roughly one-third of all food produced — is wasted each year. In wealthy nations most waste is at the consumer end; in poor nations it's mostly post-harvest losses.
The global average is about 185 liters per person per day across all uses (drinking, cooking, sanitation, agriculture). Americans use ~500 liters; many Africans survive on under 20 liters.
About 2.2 billion people lack access to safely managed drinking water. This is one of the most preventable causes of death and disease worldwide.
The average person uses about 3,300 kWh of electricity per year. Americans use ~12,000 kWh; the global average hides vast inequality — an American uses 10× more than someone in Ethiopia.
About 30% of global electricity now comes from renewable sources (hydro, wind, solar, etc.). This share is rising rapidly — wind and solar alone exceeded 13% in 2023.
About 730 million people — mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and developing Asia — still have no access to electricity. This number has fallen from 1.2 billion in 2010.
An estimated 1.6 billion people live in inadequate housing — slums, informal settlements, or without any shelter. This includes 100 million who are literally homeless.
There are roughly 1.45 billion cars on Earth — about 1 for every 5 people. But car ownership is extremely unequal: the US has ~800 cars per 1,000 people; India has about 30.

About 1.5 billion people took at least one commercial flight in 2023 (IATA). That's 150 out of every 1,000 people on Earth who fly at least once per year — flying remains a minority activity, heavily concentrated in wealthy countries.
The global average GDP per capita is about $13,500/year, but the median person earns far less. The US average is ~$65,000; the average in low-income countries is under $1,000.
The wealthiest 10% of people hold about 76% of all global wealth. The bottom 50% hold less than 2%. Wealth inequality is far more extreme than income inequality.
The world loses about 47 million hectares of forest each year — an area the size of Sweden — though reforestation efforts offset some of this.
The average person emits about 4.6 tonnes of CO₂ per year. Americans emit ~14 tonnes; people in the poorest countries emit under 0.5 tonnes — a 30× gap.
The global average life expectancy is 73 years — up from 48 in 1950. Japan leads at 84; some low-income nations are still under 60.
About 260 million children and youth are out of school. Most are in conflict-affected zones or the most remote rural areas of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
Over 114 million people are forcibly displaced — including 36 million refugees who have fled their home countries — the highest figure ever recorded.
